amendments.rule: **Hebrew has no verb *to have*, so an English *have* is a recasting and belongs to whatever made the clause possessive.** Where `הָיָה` is present it is the existential and takes the *have* itself, its preposition goes `unrepresented` under rule 40, and the suffix takes the subject pronoun: `וַיְהִי לוֹ נָשִׁים` → *he had* … *wives* puts *had* on `הָיָה` and *he* on the suffix. Where the clause is verbless, the possessive preposition is what makes it possessive and carries the *have*: `לָהֶם מִסְגְּרוֹת` → *they had panels* puts *had* on `לְ` and *they* on the suffix, and `שָׁפְרָה עָלָי` → *I have a goodly heritage* puts *have* on `עַל` and *I* on the suffix. Where neither is present, a possessive suffix can be the possession by itself and takes the supplied verb with its pronoun: `טוֹבָתִי בַּל עָלֶיךָ` → *I have no good beyond thee* gives the suffix *I have*, headed on the pronoun. Another finite verb in the clause does not qualify merely by being finite. `שָׁפְרָה` is not a copula: the ASV renders it by the attributive *goodly*, which is its lexeme, so the *have* is not its. **But a verb the ASV has itself rendered by the *have* does qualify, and the same subtraction decides it.** Where the Hebrew writes a verb of falling or allotment and the English writes *have* in its place — `יִפְּלוּ בְנַחֲלָה` → *they shall have inheritance* — dropping the word leaves that verb with no rendering at all, so the *have* is the verb's own together with the subject pronoun rule 17 keeps there, and a preposition beside it whose relation the ASV has left unstated goes `unrepresented` under rule 40. **And where nothing in the clause makes it possessive, the word is not to be placed at all.** A clause that writes no `הָיָה`, no possessive preposition, no suffix and no verb the *have* renders has no morpheme to carry it: `יוֹסֵף חֲבָלִים` → *Joseph* ***shall have two*** *portions* leaves the supplied verb its own `added` unit under rule 20's supplied-lexical-verb clause, together with any numeral, subject or object the ASV supplies alongside it, while the possessed noun keeps only its own word. Do not fold such a word into that noun, into a neighbouring clause's verb, or into a preposition standing elsewhere in the verse to avoid the `added`, for the reason rule 42 gives about a surplus *and*: it is written beside those renderings rather than inside one of them. Test by subtraction, as in rule 16 — drop the *have* and ask which morpheme has lost its rendering. If only the possession relation is gone, the *have* is the preposition's or the suffix's; if a written verb is left with nothing, it is that verb's; and if nothing in the clause is diminished but a possession the English has supplied, it is `added`. **Read *no possessive preposition* and *no suffix* in that count as none the ASV has left an English word for.** A preposition or a suffix on which the ASV has already spent its own word stands in the same position as an absent one: it is not what makes the clause possessive, and it is not a home for a second English word, exactly as rule 52 counts a preposition's function words against the morphemes that could carry them and rule 51 says a waw holding an English word of its own is not a home for a second one. What this rule's earlier sentences govern is a `בְּ` or a `לְ` that is itself the clause's predicate, for which the ASV writes no preposition at all — `אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ מוּם` → *that hath a blemish* — and not a locative or other phrase the ASV has rendered in full. `אוֹ תְבַלֻּל בְּעֵינוֹ` → *or* ***that hath*** *a blemish in his eye* writes *in* for the `בְּ`, *his* for the suffix, *eye* for the noun and *a blemish* for `תְּבַלֻּל`, so nothing is left for the *hath* to complete and it is its own `added` unit; `מְרוֹחַ אָשֶׁךְ` → ***hath his*** *stones broken* goes the same way, the adjective keeping *broken* and the noun *stones*, with the supplied *his* `added` besides under rule 18's closing sentence. Count the clause's English words against the morphemes that could carry them before reaching for one that is already spent. **And where the possessive clause is a relative clause, count the ASV's words against the morphemes that could carry them before placing the English subject.** Where the ASV writes one word for the relative and the resumption together, that word is the relative's and it supplies the subject: `אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ מוּם` → *that hath a blemish* gives *that* to `אֲשֶׁר` and *hath* to the `בְּ`, and the suffix is `unrepresented` under rule 22, since two morphemes point at the antecedent and the ASV writes one word for it. **But where the ASV writes a subject pronoun besides the relative, two English words answer to the two morphemes and neither is a surplus.** `כֹּל אֲשֶׁר לוֹ` → *all* ***that he hath*** gives *that* to `אֲשֶׁר`, *hath* to the possessive `לְ` and *he* to the suffix, which is the subject pronoun this rule's earlier sentences give it; the same clause written without a relative gives the suffix that pronoun in any case, as `מוּם בּוֹ` → *he hath a blemish* does. Count as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s, and do not mark the suffix `unrepresented` beside a written pronoun no other morpheme answers to, which would leave that pronoun `added` against rule 30 while the morpheme it realizes held nothing. A written `הָיָה` in such a clause still takes the *have* itself and leaves both the preposition and the suffix `unrepresented`: `אֲשֶׁר יִהְיֶה בּוֹ מוּם` → *that hath a blemish*. **And an interrogative particle standing in such a clause does not take the *have* either.** Where `הֲ`, or the `אִם` opening a disjunctive question, stands in a possessive clause and the ASV marks the question by fronting the possessive verb itself, that word is the possessive morpheme's under this rule's earlier sentences and the particle is `unrepresented` under rule 17's sentence on a question marked by inversion alone: `וְאִם־זְרוֹעַ כָּאֵל לָךְ` → *Or* ***hast*** *thou an arm like God* gives *hast* to the `לְ` and *thou* to its suffix, and leaves the `אִם` nothing. Rule 20's fronted-copula sentence and rule 50's reading of an interrogative existential clause reach a copula the construction supplies and an existential frame, which are words no other morpheme licenses; a *have* is neither, since this rule assigns it to the `הָיָה`, the preposition, the suffix or the verb that makes the clause possessive, and handing it to the particle would leave that morpheme holding nothing while the relation it alone carries went unrendered, against rule 2. Read what the fronted word is rather than that the clause is a question: where the ASV writes a separate question auxiliary besides the *have* — a *Do*, a *Shall* or a *Will* at the clause head — that word is the particle's under rule 17 as before, and the *have* still goes where this rule sends it.
amendments.why: Rule 43's relative-clause sentence says flatly that in a possessive relative clause the relative supplies the English subject and the resumptive suffix takes nothing. Its own rationale carries the condition that made it true — the ASV writing one word for two morphemes pointing at the antecedent — but the imperative does not, and JOS.7 met the case it had not considered twice. JOS.7.15 and JOS.7.24 both write kol 'asher lo as 'all that he hath', with a relative and a subject pronoun both written. Read flatly the sentence would mark the suffix unrepresented and leave the written 'he' answering to no morpheme, hence added under rule 30, while the suffix that realizes it held nothing — the outcome rule 2 and rule 30 forbid. The amendment makes the existing rationale operative as the count rules 42 and 52 already run elsewhere, keeps the 'asher bo mum ruling and its rule 22 grounding verbatim, and changes nothing else in the rule. The formula kol 'asher lo is common across the historical books, so the ambiguity would recur; the corpus rows carry lamed to 'had' 91 times, 'have' 40 and 'hath' 39, and rule 43's own opening examples already give a suffix the subject pronoun in a non-relative possessive clause, so nothing in the precedent pulls the other way.

conventions: JOS.7.3 compresses two Hebrew numeral phrases (ke-alpayim ish o ki-shloshet alafim ish) into one English phrase, about two or three thousand men, and the count runs word by word. The single written about stands before two, so the first comparative kaph takes it and the second is unrepresented under rule 22; the counted noun runs tail-to-tail, so the last ish takes men and the first is unrepresented; and the dual alpayim takes two while the single written thousand closes the whole figure on alafim. Read which numeral each English word stands before rather than preferring a position.

The distributive la-gevarim is divided the same way in JOS.7.14, 7.17 and 7.18: the lamed takes the by of man by man, gever takes both occurrences of man as one discontinuous unit under rule 25, and the assimilated article is unrepresented because the ASV writes no the for the phrase.

JOS.7.7 and 7.8 open the same prayer with different Hebrew, and each is divided by what the ASV wrote. In 7.7 ahah takes Alas and the vocative O joins the base noun of the divine title under rule 36. In 7.8 the entreaty particle bi takes the Oh written for it, a present morpheme taking its English before a supplied vocative reading does, and the base noun keeps the bare Lord. The 1cs suffix of the title is unrepresented in both under rule 57.

report: Checked every multi-treatment group in the candidate table. All 64 resolve to ASV differences the source licenses, not splits: the waw takes whichever connective the ASV wrote (But, for, So, therefore, when, then, yea); lakad alternates taketh and shall take because the ASV does; qarab writes 'he brought near' in 7.17-18 and a bare 'brought near' in 7.16, where Joshua is the written subject; na' takes the full 'I pray thee' in one clause and a bare 'now' in the other, which rule 30's closing sentence allows; herem is 'accursed' only in 7.12, where rule 21's resultative hayah-le puts the copula on the verb and leaves the lamed unrepresented.

Article handling is uniform chapter-wide. Every ha takes a written 'the' where one stands before its own word; is unrepresented where the phrase's single determiner is a demonstrative or a possessive another morpheme carries (7.7, 7.9, 7.21, 7.25, 7.26); and takes the fronted 'the' where the rectum is rendered anarthrously (7.4, 7.5, 7.24). The ha-'Ai correction already carried in verses 04.json and 05.json is what rule 29's proper-name paragraph directs, and it does not conflict with 7.2, 7.3 and 7.17, where no 'the' is written at all.

Read the dump for added units, which the table is blind to. The six agree with each other: a supplied 'their' on 'oreph is added in both 7.8 and 7.12, and a supplied object pronoun with no object morpheme in the clause is added in 7.9, 7.11 and 7.19. No verse folds one of these into a neighbouring rendering to avoid the added.

One near-miss I examined and left alone. JOS.7.3 marks the coordinating 'but' of 'but let about two or three thousand men go up' added while folding the restrictive 'but' of 'they are but few' into me'at's unit. These are not one construction analysed two ways: the coordinator stands between two clauses with no conjunction morpheme in the second, which rule 14's closing sentences make added, whereas the restrictive adverb stands inside me'at's own rendering with the construction-supplied copula on one side and 'few' on the other, which is the side of rule 14's subtraction test that keeps a word inside the rendering it sits in. The verse note already names the competing reading, so a later reader has what rule 8 asks for and nothing is gained by churning the edge.

BSB disagreements are all documented convention differences, and none is a genuine error. The Td and R runs are articles and prepositions the ASV leaves unrendered under rules 29, 40 and 52; the To run is the object marker under rule 16; the two Sp1cs 'my' tokens are the lexicalized suffix of 'adonai under rule 57, which the contract settles explicitly; the three Sp3ms/Sp3fs tokens in 7.14 are resumptive object suffixes on yilkedennu, which English drops entirely, so the bare relative 'which' is the whole of what is written and rule 22's first sentence governs; the 7.21 suffix on mishqalo and the 7.25 ba- both answer to English the ASV simply does not write.

One amendment to rule 43, no promotions. This chapter twice wrote 'all that he hath' for kol 'asher lo, where the ASV writes both a relative and a subject pronoun; rule 43's relative-clause sentence, read as it stands, would send the suffix to unrepresented and leave the written 'he' with no morpheme to answer to.
